'But why speak of a ship? — for I saw the oar despised by you: greater things, perhaps, you seek. What can be greater than the sun, which the mathematicians affirm to be more than eighteen times larger than the earth? How small it seems to us! To me indeed about a foot across; but Epicurus thinks it may even be smaller than it appears, though not by much; nor does he think it much larger, but either just so great as it appears, so that the eyes either do not lie at all or do not lie much — yet they do lie: where, then, is that "once"? But let us leave this credulous man, who thinks the senses never lie — who not even now, when that sun, which is borne with so great a rush that how great its swiftness is cannot even be conceived, yet seems to us to stand still.'

'But, that I may lessen the controversy, see, I pray, in how small a matter the dispute lies. There are four heads which would conclude that there is nothing which can be known, perceived, comprehended — about which is this whole question. Of these the first is that there is some false impression; the second, that this cannot be perceived; the third, that among impressions between which there is no difference, it cannot happen that some of them can be perceived and others not; the fourth, that there is no true impression proceeding from a sense to which is not attached another impression which differs from it in nothing and which cannot be perceived. Of these four heads all concede the second and the third; the first Epicurus does not grant; you, with whom we have to do, concede that too; the whole battle is about the fourth.'

'He, therefore, who saw Publius Servilius Geminus, if he thought he saw Quintus, fell upon an impression of such a kind that it could not be perceived, because by no mark was the true distinguished from the false; and that distinction being taken away, what mark could he have in recognizing Gaius Cotta, who was twice consul with Geminus, of such a kind as could not be false? You deny that there is so great a likeness in the nature of things; you fight altogether, but with an easy adversary. Grant that there is not: it can certainly seem so; it will therefore deceive the sense. And if one likeness shall have deceived, it will have rendered all things doubtful; for that judgement being taken away by which it is right to recognize, even if it shall be the very man whom you see who appears to you, yet you will not judge by that mark by which you say one ought, so that there cannot be a false one of the same kind.'

'When, therefore, Publius Geminus can seem to you to be Quintus, what have you ascertained why Cotta cannot seem to you to be one who is not, since something seems to be that is not? You say all things are of their own kind, and nothing is the same as something else. That indeed is Stoic, and not very credible — that there is no hair like another hair in all things, no grain like another grain. These things can be refuted, but I do not wish to fight; for, as to the matter at issue, it makes no difference whether, the thing being seen, the impression differs in no part, or cannot be distinguished even if it differs. But if there cannot be so great a likeness of men, can there not even of statues? Tell me: could not Lysippus, with the same bronze, the same tempering, the same graver, water, and all else, make a hundred Alexanders of the same kind? By what notion, then, would you distinguish them?'

'What if I shall stamp in wax of such a kind a hundred seals with this signet-ring? Can there be any distinction in recognizing them? Or will you have to seek out some ring-maker, since you found that man of Delos who kept hens, to recognize the eggs? But you bring in art summoned even to the aid of the senses: "the painter sees what we do not see," and "as soon as the flute-player has breathed, the tune is recognized by the skilled." What of this? Does it not seem to tell against you, if, without great arts, to which few attain — of our kind indeed very few — we can neither see nor hear? Now that famous matter — with how great a craft nature has fashioned our senses and mind and the whole construction of man —'

'why should I not dread the rashness of opinion? Can you even affirm this, Lucullus, that there is some force, with prudence and counsel forsooth, which has fashioned, or, to use your own word, which has fabricated man? Of what kind is that workmanship, where applied, when, why, in what manner? These things are ingeniously handled, even elegantly argued; finally, let them seem so, only let them not be affirmed. But of the natural philosophers presently — and indeed for this reason, lest you, who said a little before that I would do this, should seem to have lied. But, that I may come to things which are clearer, I will now pour forth whole subjects, about which volumes have been filled, not only by our men but even by Chrysippus (about whom the Stoics are wont to complain that, while he zealously sought out everything against the senses and clearness, and against all common usage and against reason, he was, in answering himself, the weaker — and so by him Carneades was armed);'

'these are of such a kind as have been most diligently handled by you. You said that the impressions of sleepers and drunkards and madmen are weaker than those of the waking, the sober, the sane. How so? Because when Ennius was awake he would not say that he had seen Homer, but that he seemed to; and Alcmeon, "but in no way does my heart agree"; the like about drunkards. As though anyone denied either that he who is awake does not dream, or that he whose madness has subsided thinks the things were not true which seemed to him in his madness. But that is not the point; the question is, at the time when they were seen, how they were seen. Unless indeed we think that Ennius did not so hear that whole "O piety of soul" — if only he dreamed it — as if he had heard it waking. For awake he could think those impressions to be, what they were, dreams; but to the sleeper they were approved equally as to the waking. What of Ilione in that sleep, "Mother, I call you" — does she not so believe her son spoke as she would believe even when awake? For whence those words, "come, stand, stay, hear; repeat those same things to me again"? Does she seem to have less confidence in the impressions than the waking?'

'What shall I say of the mad? Of what kind, pray, was your kinsman, Catulus, Tuditanus? Does anyone, however sane, think the things he sees as certain as that man thought the things that appeared to him? What of him who said, "I see, I see you; live, Ulysses, while you may" — did he not even twice cry out that he saw, when he did not see at all? What of Hercules in Euripides, when, as he pierced the sons of Eurystheus, so he pierced his own with arrows, when he slew his wife, when he tried even to slay his father — was he not moved by false things just as he would be moved by true? What of your own Alcmeon, who denies that his heart agrees with his eyes — does he not in the same place, his madness roused, cry, "whence rises this flame?" and then those words next, "they come on, they come on, they are here, they seek me"? And when he implores the maiden's faith: "bring me aid, drive off the plague from me, this flame-bearing force which tortures me; girt with a dark serpent they advance, they stand around with burning torches" — do you doubt that he seems to himself to see these things? And likewise the rest: "long-haired Apollo bends his golden bow, leaning on the moon; Diana hurls a torch from the left."'

'How would he believe these things more if they were than he believed because they appeared? For it is plain now that his heart agrees with his eyes. And all these things are brought forward in order that this may be made out — than which nothing can be more certain — that between true and false impressions, as regards the assent of the mind, there is no difference. But you accomplish nothing when you refute those false impressions of madmen or dreamers by their own recollection. For it is not asked of what kind the recollection is wont to be of those who have awakened or of those who have ceased to rave, but of what kind the vision was either of the raving or of the dreaming at the time when they were moved by it.'

'But I depart from the senses. What is there that can be perceived by reason? You say that dialectic was invented as the arbiter, as it were, and judge of true and false. Of what true and false, and in what matter? In geometry will the dialectician judge what is true or false, or in letters, or in music? But he does not know those things. In philosophy, then: how great the sun is, what is that to him? What has he by which he can judge what is the highest good? What, then, will he judge? Which conjunction, which disjunction is true; what has been said ambiguously; what follows each thing and what is repugnant: if he judges these and the like, he judges about himself; but he promised more. For to judge these things is not enough for the rest of the matters which are in philosophy, many and great.'

'But since you place so much in that art, see lest it has been wholly born against you; which, having first advanced pleasantly, hands down the elements of speech and the understanding of ambiguities and the method of concluding, then, with a few things added, comes to the sorites, a slippery and dangerous place indeed — which you just now said was a faulty kind of questioning. What, then, of that fault — is it our fault? The nature of things has given us no cognition of limits, so that in any matter we can determine how far; nor only in this heap of wheat, whence the name comes, but in no matter at all, being questioned little by little — whether one is rich, poor, famous, obscure; many, few, great, small, long, short, broad, narrow — by how much, either added or taken away, we may answer for certain, we have no means of knowing.'

'"But sorites are faulty." Break them, then, if you can, that they may not be troublesome; for they will be, unless you beware. "It has been guarded against," he says; "for it pleases Chrysippus, when one is questioned step by step — for example, whether three are few or many — to keep quiet somewhat before he comes to many" (that is what is called by these men hesychazein, to be still). "For all I care, you may snore," says Carneades, "not merely keep quiet. But what does it profit? For there follows one who rouses you from sleep and questions you in the same way: 'at what number you fell silent, if to that number I add one, will they be many?' You will advance again as far as it seems good." Why say more? For you confess this, that you can answer neither the last of the few nor the first of the many. An error of this kind so spreads that I do not see whither it cannot reach.'

'"It does me no harm," he says; "for, like a skilful charioteer, before I come to the end I will hold in my horses, and the more so if the place to which the horses are borne shall be precipitous. So," he says, "I hold myself in beforehand, and answer no longer to one questioning captiously." If you have something that is clear and do not answer, that is haughty; if you have not, then you yourself do not perceive. If because it is obscure, I grant it; but you deny that you advance as far as obscure things; in clear matters, then, you stop. If only so that you may be silent, you accomplish nothing; for what is it to him who wishes to ensnare you, whether he entangles you silent or speaking? But if you answer without doubt, for example, up to nine, that they are few, and at the tenth stop, you withhold assent even from things certain and clearer; this same thing in obscure matters you do not allow me to do. That art, then, helps you nothing against the sorites, which teaches neither what, in increasing or diminishing, is first nor what is last.'

'What of this — that that same art, unweaving as it were the web of Penelope, takes away at the end what went before: is that your fault or ours? Surely the foundation of dialectic is that whatever is stated (and this they call axioma, which is as it were an assertion) is either true or false. What, then, are these true or false: "if you say that you are lying and you say this truly, you are lying; you speak truly"? These things, of course, you say are inexplicable; which is more odious than those which we call not comprehended and not perceived — but this I pass over. This I ask: if those things cannot be explained, nor is any judgement of them found, so that you can answer whether they are true or false, where is that definition, that an assertion is that which is either true or false? Things being assumed, I will add that from them some must be inferred and others rejected which are in the contrary class.'

'In what way, then, do you judge this to have been concluded: "if you say it is now light and you say truly, it is light; but you say it is now light and you say truly; it is light therefore"? You certainly approve the form and say it is most rightly concluded, and so in teaching you hand down this first as a mode of concluding. Either, then, you will approve whatever is concluded in the same way, or that art is nothing. See, therefore, whether you will approve this conclusion: "if you say you are lying and you say truly, you are lying; but you say you are lying and you say truly; you are lying therefore." How can you not approve this, when you have approved the earlier one of the same kind? These things are Chrysippus's, not resolved even by himself. For what would he do with this conclusion, "if it is light, it is light; but it is light; it is light therefore"? He would yield, of course; for the very reasoning of the connected proposition, when you have conceded the antecedent, compels you to concede the consequent. How, then, does this differ from that conclusion, "if you are lying, you are lying; but you are lying; you are lying therefore"? This you deny that you can either approve or disapprove; how, then, the other any the more? If art, if reason, if method, if in fine the force of the conclusion holds good, it is the same in both.'

'But this is their last resort: they demand that these inexplicables be excepted. Let them look for some tribune, I advise; that exception they will never obtain from me. For when from Epicurus, who both despises and mocks the whole of dialectic, they cannot obtain that he concede the truth of what we shall thus state, "either Hermarchus will be alive tomorrow or he will not be alive," while the dialecticians thus determine that everything which is so disjoined as "either yes or no" is not only true but even necessary (see how cautious is the man whom those people think dull: "for if," he says, "I shall have conceded either to be necessary, it will be necessary that Hermarchus tomorrow either be alive or not be alive; but there is no such necessity in the nature of things") — when, then, the dialecticians fight with this man, that is, Antiochus and the Stoics — for he overthrows the whole of dialectic; for if a disjunction of contraries (and I call those contrary, when one affirms, the other denies) — if such a disjunction can be false, none is true.'

'But what disputes have they with me, who follow their own school? When anything of this kind had occurred, Carneades was wont to jest thus: "if I have concluded rightly, I keep my ground; but if faultily, Diogenes shall give back my mina"; for he had learned dialectic from that Stoic, and this was the fee of the dialecticians. I follow, then, those paths which I learned from Antiochus, nor do I find how I should judge "if it is light, it is light" to be true for this reason, because I so learned, that everything which is connected of itself is true, and not judge "if you are lying, you are lying" to be connected in the same way: either, then, this as that, or, unless this, not even that shall I judge. But, that we may leave all those stings and the whole tortuous kind of arguing, and may show what we are, the whole opinion of Carneades being now explained, all those Antiochean things will collapse together. Nor indeed shall I say anything in such a way that anyone may suspect it is invented; I will take it from Clitomachus, who was with Carneades even to old age, a man both acute, as a Carthaginian, and very zealous and diligent; and there are four books of his on the withholding of assents, but these things which I shall now say are taken from the first.'

'It pleases Carneades that there are two kinds of impressions; in the one this division, that some impressions are such as can be perceived and others such as cannot; in the other, that some impressions are probable and others not probable. And so the things which are said against the senses and against clearness pertain to the former division; against the latter nothing ought to be said. Wherefore he holds thus — that no impression is such that perception follows, but that approval follows many. For it would be against nature, if nothing were probable; there follows that overthrow of all life which you, Lucullus, were mentioning. And so many things even of the senses must be approved, provided only that this be held — that there is in them nothing of such a kind as a false one differing in nothing from it could not also be; thus whatever shall occur probable in appearance, if nothing shall present itself contrary to that probability, the wise man will use it, and thus the whole reason of life will be governed. And indeed even he who is brought in by you as the wise man follows many probabilities not comprehended nor perceived nor assented to, but like the truth, which unless he should approve, the whole of life would be taken away.'

'For when the wise man embarks upon a ship, has he comprehended in his mind and perceived that he will sail according to his purpose? How can he? But if now he should set out from this place for Puteoli, thirty stadia, in a sound vessel with a good helmsman in this calm, it would seem probable that he will arrive there safe. By impressions of this kind, then, he will take his counsels of acting and not acting, and will be readier to approve that snow is white than was Anaxagoras, who not only denied that it is so, but, because he knew that the water from which it was congealed is black, denied that it even seems white;'

'and whatever thing shall so touch him that the impression is probable and impeded by nothing, he will be moved. For he is not carved from rock or hewn from oak; he has a body, he has a mind; he is moved in mind, he is moved in his senses, so that many things seem to him true, and yet he does not have that distinguishing and proper mark of perceiving. And on that account the wise man does not assent, because there can arise something false of the same kind as this true thing is. Nor do we speak against the senses otherwise than the Stoics, who say that many things are false and stand far otherwise than they appear to the senses. But if this be so, that even one thing appears false to the senses, there is at hand one to deny that any thing can be perceived by the senses. So, with us silent, from one head of Epicurus and another of yours, perception and comprehension are taken away. What is the head of Epicurus? "If any impression of a sense is false, nothing can be perceived." What is yours? "There are false impressions of the senses." What follows? Though I be silent, the conclusion itself speaks: "nothing can be perceived." "I do not concede it," he says, "to Epicurus." Contend then with him, who is wholly opposed to you; do not contend with me, who in this at least certainly — that there is something false in the senses — agree with you.'

'And yet nothing seems to me so strange as that these things are said, and by Antiochus above all, to whom those things were most familiar which I said a little before. For anyone may by his own judgement reprove this — that we deny anything can be perceived; the reproach is certainly lighter, in that we nevertheless say that certain things are probable. This does not seem enough to you. Let it not be; those things at least we ought to escape which were most agitated by you: "You discern nothing, then, you hear nothing, nothing is clear to you." I explained a little before, on Clitomachus's authority, in what way Carneades said these things; hear in what way the same things are said by Clitomachus in that book which he wrote to Gaius Lucilius the poet, when he had written on the same matters to Lucius Censorinus, the one who was consul with Manius Manilius. He wrote, then, in nearly these words (for they are known to me, because in that book is contained the first instruction and as it were teaching of those very matters about which we are dealing) — but it is written thus:—'

'that it pleases the Academics that there are such dissimilarities of things that some seem probable and others the contrary; but that this is not enough for you to say that some can be perceived and others cannot, because many false things are probable, but nothing false can be perceived and known. And so he says that those greatly err who say that the senses are taken away by the Academy, by whom it was never said that either colour or taste or sound is nothing; this was argued — that there is not in them that proper mark of the true and the certain which exists nowhere else.'

'When he had set forth these things, he adds that the wise man is said in two ways to withhold assent: in one way, when this is understood, that he assents to no thing at all; in the other, when he withholds himself from answering, so as either to approve or disapprove something, so that he neither denies nor affirms anything. This being so, the one pleases him — that he should never assent; the other he holds — that, following probability, wherever it either occurs or fails, he may answer either "yes" or "no." And since it pleases that he who restrains himself from assenting about all things is nevertheless moved and does something, he leaves impressions of such a kind by which we are roused to action, likewise those to which, being questioned, we can answer on either side, following only what so appears, provided it be without assent; nor yet that all impressions of such a kind are approved, but those which are impeded by nothing.'

'If we do not prove these things to you, let them be false, granted; invidious they certainly are not. For we do not snatch away the light, but those things which you say are perceived and comprehended, those same we say seem to us — provided only they be probable. Thus, the probable being introduced and established — and that indeed unencumbered, free, loose, involved in nothing — you surely see, Lucullus, that that patronage of yours of clearness now lies prostrate. For this wise man of whom I speak will behold the sky, the earth, the sea with the same eyes with which that wise man of yours does, and will perceive with the same senses the rest of the things which fall under each sense. That sea, which now, with the west wind rising, seems purple, will seem the same to this man of ours, and yet he will not assent, because to us ourselves a little while ago it seemed dark blue in the morning, grey; and that part which now, where it is lit by the sun, grows white and quivers, and is unlike the part next to it — so that, even if you can give the reason why this comes about, you cannot yet maintain that to be true which appeared to the eyes.'

'"Whence comes memory, if we perceive nothing?" — for so you used to ask. What, can we not remember impressions except those comprehended? What of Polyaenus, who is said to have been a great mathematician, who afterward, assenting to Epicurus, believed the whole of geometry to be false — did he forget even those things which he knew? But what is false cannot be perceived, as you yourselves hold. If, then, memory is of things perceived and comprehended, all that anyone remembers he holds comprehended and perceived; but nothing false can be comprehended; and Siro remembers all the dogmas of Epicurus; therefore those things are now all true. This, for all I care, may stand; but you must either concede that it is so — which you least of all wish — or grant me memory and confess that there is a place for it even if there be no comprehension and perception.'

'"What will become of the arts?" Of which? Of those which themselves confess that they use conjecture more than knowledge, or of those which only follow what appears, and have not that art of yours by which they distinguish true and false? But there are those two lights which most of all contain that cause of yours. For first you deny that it can happen that anyone assents to no thing. But this indeed is clear, since Panaetius, almost the chief of the Stoics in my judgement at least, says that he doubts about that matter which all the Stoics except him think most certain — that the responses of soothsayers, auspices, oracles, dreams, prophecies are true — and withholds himself from assent: which since he can do even about those matters which they from whom he himself learned held certain, why cannot the wise man do this about the rest? Or is there something which, being laid down, he can either disapprove or approve, but cannot doubt? Or will you be able to stop in the sorites when you wish, while he cannot stop in the rest of matters in the same way — especially when he can, without assent, follow the very likeness of truth that is unimpeded?'

'The other point is that you deny that there can be action of any thing in him who approves no thing by his assent. For first something must be seen, in which there is also assent (for the Stoics say that the senses themselves are assents, which, since appetite follows, action follows) — but that all things are taken away if impressions are taken away. On this matter much has been both said and written on both sides; but the whole thing can be settled briefly. For I, although I think it the greatest action to fight against impressions, to resist opinions, to withhold assents that are slippery — and I believe Clitomachus, who writes thus, that a certain labour of Hercules was performed by Carneades, in that, like a wild and savage beast, he had drawn out from our minds assent, that is, opinion and rashness — yet, that this part of the defence may be left aside, what shall impede the action of him who follows probabilities with nothing impeding?'

'"This very thing," he says, "will impede him — that he will determine that not even that which he approves can be perceived." Now this will impede you too in sailing and in sowing, in taking a wife and in begetting children, and in very many matters, in which you follow nothing but the probable. And yet you bring up that worn and oft-rejected argument, not as Antipater did, but, as you say, more pointedly; for Antipater was reproved for saying that it is consistent for him who affirms that nothing can be comprehended to say at least that this very thing can be comprehended. This seemed gross to Antiochus himself and self-contradictory; for it cannot be said consistently that nothing can be comprehended, if it be said that anything can be comprehended. He thinks Carneades should rather have been pressed in this way — that, since no decree of the wise man can exist unless comprehended, perceived, known, he who said that this very decree is the wise man's, that nothing can be perceived, should confess that it has been perceived. Just as if the wise man had no other decree and could lead his life without decrees.'

'But as he holds those things probable, not perceived, so this very thing — that nothing can be perceived. For if in this he had a mark of cognition, he would use the same in the rest; since he has it not, he uses probabilities. And so he does not fear lest he seem to confound all things and render them uncertain. For not in the way that, if it be asked of him whether the number of the stars is even or odd, so also, if about duty and many other matters in which he is versed and practised, he would say that he does not know. For in uncertain things there is nothing probable; but in those in which there is, in them there will be wanting to the wise man neither what he should do nor what he should answer.'

'You did not pass over even that reproach of Antiochus, Lucullus (nor was it strange, for it is among the most famous), by which Antiochus used to say that Philo was most of all confounded. For when it was assumed, in the one premise, that certain impressions are false, in the other, that they differ in nothing from the true, he did not attend to this — that the former premise was conceded for the reason that there seemed to be a certain difference in impressions, and that this was taken away by the other, in which he denies that true impressions differ from false — nothing being so repugnant. This would be so, if we took away the true altogether. We do not; for we discern things true as well as false. But there is an appearance of approving, of perceiving we have no sign.'

'And I seem to myself even now to be acting too meagrely. For since there is a field in which discourse might exult, why do we drive it into such straits and into the brambles of the Stoics? For if I had to do with a Peripatetic, who said that what was stamped from the true could be perceived, and that there did not adhere that great addition, "in such a way that it could not be stamped from the false," I should deal simply with a simple man, nor should I greatly contend; and even if, when I said that nothing could be comprehended, he said that the wise man sometimes holds an opinion, I should not resist — especially since not even Carneades strongly resists this point. As it is, what can I do? For I ask what there is that can be comprehended.'

'There answers me not Aristotle or Theophrastus, not even Xenocrates or Polemo, but these lesser men, that a truth is of such a kind as a falsehood could not be. I find nothing of that kind: therefore, doubtless, I shall assent to the unknown, that is, I shall hold an opinion. This both the Peripatetics and the Old Academy concede me; you deny it, Antiochus above all. He moves me greatly, both because I loved the man as he did me, and because I so judge — the most polished and acute of all the philosophers of our memory. Of whom I ask first, in what manner, pray, he is of that Academy of which he professes to be. To pass over other things, of these two matters at issue, who ever said, either of the Old Academy or of the Peripatetics, either that that alone could be perceived which was a truth of such a kind as a falsehood could not be, or that the wise man holds no opinion? Certainly no one. Neither of these was strongly defended before Zeno; I, however, think both true, nor do I say so for the occasion, but I plainly approve them so.'

'This I cannot bear: that you, when you forbid me to assent to the unknown, and say that this is most base and most full of rashness, should arrogate so much to yourself as to set forth the doctrine of wisdom, to unfold the nature of all things, to fashion characters, to establish the ends of good and evil, to describe duties, to define what life I am to enter upon, and at the same time to say that you will hand down a criterion and an art of arguing and understanding — will you bring it about that I, embracing those innumerable things, should nowhere slip, should hold no opinion? What, pray, is that doctrine to which you would lead me, if you should draw me away from this one? I fear you act somewhat arrogantly if you say "your own"; and yet you must necessarily say so. Nor indeed you alone, but each man will snatch me to his own.'

'Come — should I withstand the Peripatetics, who say that they have a kinship with orators, who say that illustrious men trained by them have often governed the commonwealth; should I hold out against the Epicureans, so many of my friends, men so good, so loving toward one another; what shall I do with Diodotus the Stoic, whom I heard from boyhood, who lives with me so many years, who dwells in my house, whom I both admire and love, who despises those Antiochean things? "Ours alone," you will say, "are true." Certainly alone, if true; for there cannot be several true things at variance with each other. Are we, then, the shameless ones, who do not wish to slip, or they the arrogant, who have persuaded themselves that they alone know all things? "Not I indeed," he says, "but the wise man, I say, knows." Excellent: namely, knows those things which are in your doctrine. What is this in the first place — that wisdom is explained by one who is not wise? But let us depart from our own selves, let us speak of the wise man, about whom, as I have often said already, is this whole question.'

'Into three parts, then, both by most men and by your own selves, is wisdom divided. First, then, let us see, if you please, what has been inquired about the nature of things — or, as before: is there anyone puffed up with so great an error as to have persuaded himself that he knows those things? I do not seek those reasonings which depend on conjecture, which are dragged this way and that by discussions, and bring no necessity of persuading; let the geometers see to it, who profess not to persuade but to compel, and who prove to you all the things they describe. I do not seek from them those first principles of the mathematicians, which not being conceded they cannot advance a finger's breadth: that a point is that which has no magnitude, an extremity and as it were a boundary in which there is no thickness at all, a line a length without any breadth. When I shall have conceded these to be true, if I should put the wise man to his oath — and not before Archimedes, while he looks on, has described all those reasonings by which it is made out that the sun is many times larger than the earth — do you think he would swear? If he should do so, he would have despised the sun itself, which he thinks to be a god.'

'But if he is not going to believe geometrical reasonings, which bring force in teaching, as you yourselves say, that man will be far from believing the arguments of the philosophers — or, if he is going to believe, those of which men's especially? For one may unfold all the views of the natural philosophers, but it is long; yet I ask whom he follows. Suppose someone now becomes wise, is not yet so; what opinion and doctrine will he choose by preference? And yet whatever he shall choose, he will choose as a fool; but let him be of divine genius: which one of the natural philosophers will he most approve? Nor will he be able to approve more than one. I do not pursue the infinite questions; only about the first principles of things, of which all things consist, let us see whom he approves; for among great men there is the highest dissension.'

'Thales, the chief, one of the seven, to whom the remaining six are said to have yielded the first place, said that all things consist of water. But he did not persuade Anaximander, his fellow-citizen and companion, of this; for he said that the infinity of nature was that from which all things were begotten. Afterward his pupil Anaximenes said that the air was infinite, but that the things which arose from it were finite; and that earth, water, fire were begotten, then from these all things. Anaxagoras said matter was infinite, but that from it there were minute particles like one another, these at first confused, afterward brought into order by a divine mind. Xenophanes, a little earlier even, said that all things were one, and that this was not changeable, and that this was god, never born and everlasting, of a spherical figure. Parmenides said it was fire which moves, earth which is formed by it. Leucippus, the full and the void. Democritus is in this like him, but richer in the rest. Empedocles those four well-known and familiar elements. Heraclitus, fire. Melissus, that which was infinite and unchangeable, and had been always and would be. Plato thinks that the world was made by a god out of matter receiving all things into itself, and is everlasting. The Pythagoreans wish all things to proceed from numbers and the first principles of the mathematicians. Out of these your wise man will choose, I suppose, some one whom he will follow; the rest, so many and so great men, rejected and condemned by him, will depart.'

'But whatever opinion he shall have approved, he will so hold it comprehended in his mind as the things which he holds by the senses; nor will he any more approve that it is now light than, since he is a Stoic, that this world is wise, that it has a mind which has fashioned both itself and the world and moderates, moves, rules all things; he will be persuaded too that the sun, moon, all the stars, the earth, the sea are gods, because a certain animate intelligence pervades and passes through all those things; yet that there will be a time when this whole world shall blaze up with fire. Let those things be true (for you now laugh that I confess there is something true), yet I deny that they are comprehended and perceived. For when that Stoic wise man of yours has told you those things syllable by syllable, there will come Aristotle pouring forth a golden river of speech, who says that he raves; for the world was never born, because there was no beginning of so glorious a work upon any new counsel taken; and it is so fitted together on every side that no force can contrive such great motions and change, no old age arise through length of time that this fair order should ever fall away and perish. For you it will be necessary to reject this, but to defend that earlier view as your head and reputation: am I not left even to doubt?'

'To pass over the levity of those who assent rashly, of how great worth is liberty itself — that it is not necessary for me what is necessary for you. For I ask why god, when he made all things for our sake (for so you wish), made so great a quantity of water-snakes and vipers, why he scattered so many deadly and pernicious things over land and sea. You deny that these could be wrought so finely and so subtly without some divine skill; whose majesty indeed you bring down even to the perfection of bees and ants, so that there might seem to have been even among the gods some Myrmecides, a fashioner of tiny little works.'

'You deny that anything can be without a god: behold, there comes at you from the flank Strato of Lampsacus, who would grant to that god of yours an exemption — a great gift indeed; but since the priests of the gods have a dispensation, how much fairer that the gods themselves should have one. He denies that he uses the labour of the gods for fashioning the world, and teaches that all things, whatever they be, have been wrought by nature — not, like that other man, who says these things are concreted of rough and smooth and hooked and crooked bodies with void interposed: he thinks these are the dreams of Democritus, not teaching but wishing; but he himself, pursuing the single parts of the world, teaches that whatever either is or comes to be, comes to be or has been made by natural weights and motions. Truly that man both frees god from a great labour and frees me from fear. For who, when he thinks himself cared for by a god, can fail both day and night to dread the divine power, and, if anything adverse has happened — which has happened to whom does it not? — to be afraid lest it have come about by justice? Yet I assent neither to Strato nor indeed to you; now this, now that seems more probable.'

'All these things lie hidden, Lucullus, concealed and surrounded by thick darkness, so that no keenness of human genius is so great as to be able to penetrate into the sky, to enter into the earth. We do not know our own bodies; what is the position of the parts, what power each part has we are ignorant; and so the physicians themselves, whose interest it was to know these things, laid them open that they might be seen, nor do the empirics say that these things are on that account more known, because it may happen that, laid bare and uncovered, they are changed. But can we in the same way dissect, lay open, divide the natures of things, so as to see whether the earth is fixed deep down and clings as it were by its own roots, or hangs in the midst?'

'Xenophanes says that the moon is inhabited, and that it is an earth of many cities and mountains: these seem portents; but yet neither could he who said it swear that it is so, nor I that it is not. You too say that there are men over against us, on the contrary part of the earth, who stand with feet opposed to our feet, whom you call antipodes: why are you more angry with me, who do not spurn those things, than with those who, when they hear them, think you are out of your minds? Hicetas of Syracuse, as Theophrastus says, thinks that the sky, sun, moon, stars, and in fine all the things above stand still, and that nothing in the world is moved except the earth; which, since it turns and twists about its axis with the highest swiftness, all the same things are brought about as if, the earth standing still, the heaven were moved. And some think that Plato too says this in the Timaeus, but a little more obscurely. What of you, Epicurus, speak: do you think the sun so small? "I? For us indeed it is just so great." And you are mocked by him, and you yourselves in turn make sport of him. Free, then, from such mockery is Socrates, free Aristo of Chios, who think that none of these things can be known.'

'But I return to the soul and the body. Are these things at last well enough known to us — what the nature of the nerves is, what of the veins? Do we grasp what the soul is, where it is, in fine whether it is, or, as it seemed to Dicaearchus, is not at all? If it is, whether it has three parts, as it pleased Plato, of reason, of anger, of desire, or is simple and one; if simple, whether it is fire, or breath, or blood, or, as Xenocrates held, a number without any body — which can scarcely be understood of what kind it is; and, whatever it is, whether it is mortal or eternal, for on either side many things are said. Of these some one thing seems certain to your wise man; to ours not even what is most probable occurs; so equal in most matters are the weights of contrary reasonings.'

'But if you act more modestly and accuse me not because I do not assent to your reasonings but because I assent to none, I will conquer my mind and choose someone to assent to — whom in particular, whom? Democritus; for, as you know, I was always a lover of nobility. Now I shall be pressed by the reproach of you all: "Can you either think that there is any void, when all things are so filled and crammed that both the body which is moved gives way to bodies, and wherever each thing has given way another follows immediately into its place; or that there are any atoms, from which whatever is produced is most unlike them; or that anything excellent can be produced without some mind? And, when in one world this order is so wonderful, that there are innumerable worlds above, below, on the right, on the left, before, behind, some unlike, some of the same kind; and that, as we now are at Bauli and look upon Puteoli, so there are innumerable men in like places, with the same names, honours, deeds, geniuses, forms, ages, disputing about the same matters; and that, if now, or even if while sleeping, we seem to see something in the mind, images from without break into our minds through the body. Do you not adopt those things, nor assent to fabricated matters; to feel nothing is better than to feel things so perverse."'

'It is not, then, the point that I should approve something by my assent, but that you should beware lest you demand the same things which you do, even shamelessly, not only arrogantly — especially since those things of yours do not seem to me even probable. For I think there is no divination, which you approve; and that fate by which you say all things are bound together I despise; nor do I think that this world was built by divine counsel. And perhaps it may be so; but why am I dragged into ill-will? Is it allowed me, by your leave, not to know what I do not know, or for the Stoics themselves to dispute among themselves, when it shall not be allowed to me? To Zeno and nearly all the rest of the Stoics the highest god seems to be the aether, endowed with a mind by which all things are ruled; Cleanthes, who is as it were a Stoic of the greater clans, the pupil of Zeno, thinks that the sun rules and holds power over things: so we are compelled, by the dissension of the wise, not to know our own lord, since we know not whether we serve the sun or the aether. But the magnitude of the sun (for he himself here, all radiant, seems to look at me, warning me to make frequent mention of him) — you, then, report the magnitude of this body as if you had measured it with a ten-foot rod; I refuse to trust your measure, as one trusts bad architects: is it doubtful which of us, to put it gently, is the more modest?'

'Nor yet do I think these questions of the natural philosophers ought to be banished. For the consideration and contemplation of nature is a kind of natural pasture, as it were, of minds and geniuses: we are raised up, we seem to become loftier, we look down on human things, and, thinking of the upper and heavenly things, we despise these our own as scanty and trivial. The very investigation of things both greatest and most hidden has a delight; but if anything occurs that seems like the truth, the mind is filled with the most human pleasure. This, then, both your wise man and this one of ours will inquire into.'

'But yours so as to assent, believe, affirm; ours so as to fear to hold an opinion rashly, and to think it goes excellently with him if in matters of this kind he has found what is like the truth. Let us come now to the notion of good and evil; but first a little must be said. The natural philosophers do not seem to me to consider, when they affirm those things very strongly, that they lose the authority even of those matters which seem more clear. For they no more assent and approve that it is now light than, when a crow has croaked, that it then either orders or forbids something; nor will they more affirm that that statue is six feet, if they shall have measured it, than that the sun, which they cannot measure, is more than eighteen times larger than the earth. Whence arises that conclusion: "if the sun cannot be perceived how great it is; he who approves the rest in the same way as he approves the magnitude of the sun does not perceive those things; but the magnitude of the sun cannot be perceived; he, then, who approves it as if he perceived it, perceives no thing." They will answer that it can be perceived how great the sun is: I will not resist, provided only they say that the rest are perceived and comprehended in the same way. For they cannot say that one thing is more or less comprehended than another, since of all things there is one definition of comprehending.'

'But, as I had begun: what have we ascertained in matters good and evil? Surely ends must be established to which the sum of both goods and evils may be referred. On what matter, then, is there a greater dissension among the highest men? And I omit those views which now seem abandoned — Herillus, who places the highest good in cognition and knowledge; who, though he was a pupil of Zeno, you see how greatly he dissented from him, and how not much from Plato. Noble was the school of the Megarians, of which, as I see it written, the chief was Xenophanes, whom I just now named, then Parmenides and Zeno following him (and so by these they were called the Eleatic philosophers), afterward Euclides, a pupil of Socrates, of Megara, from whom those same were called Megarians, who said that that alone is good which is one and like and the same always; these too took much from Plato. From Menedemus, however — because he was of Eretria — they were called Eretrians, whose whole good was placed in the mind and in the keenness of mind by which the truth was discerned — things like those of Herillus, but, I suppose, explained more richly and more ornately.'

'If we despise these and now think them cast aside, those at least we ought to despise less: Aristo, who, when he had been a pupil of Zeno, approved in fact those things which that man approved in words — that nothing is good except virtue, nor evil except what is contrary to virtue; he thought that in the things between there were none of those weights which Zeno wished there to be. For this man the highest good is to be moved to neither side in those matters — which is by himself called adiaphoria (indifference). But Pyrrho held that the wise man does not even feel those things — which is named apatheia (impassivity). These, then, and so many opinions let us pass over; let us look at these, which now have been long and much defended.'

'Others have wished pleasure to be the end, of whom the chief was Aristippus, who had heard Socrates — whence the Cyrenaics — afterward Epicurus, whose school is now better known, yet not agreeing with the Cyrenaics about pleasure itself. But Callipho judged that pleasure and honour are the ends; freedom from all distress, Hieronymus; this same thing joined with honour, Diodorus — both these Peripatetics. But to live honourably, enjoying those things which nature first reconciles to man, the Old Academy too judged, as the writings of Polemo show, whom Antiochus most approves, and Aristotle and his friends seem to come very near to this. Carneades too introduced — not that he approved it, but that he might oppose it to the Stoics — that the highest good is to enjoy those things which nature first reconciled to us. But to live honourably, which is derived from the reconciliation of nature, Zeno, who was the inventor and chief of the Stoics, established to be the end of goods.'

'Now this is plain — that, to all those ends of goods which I have set forth, the ends of evils are contrary. To you now I refer the question whom I should follow; only let no one give that answer so unlearned and absurd, "any one you please, only some one": nothing can be said more inconsiderate. I desire to follow the Stoics. Is it allowed — I omit by way of Aristotle, in my judgement nearly unique in philosophy — by way of Antiochus himself, who was called an Academic, though he was, if he had changed very few things, a most genuine Stoic? The matter, then, will now be at a crisis; for either the wise man must be set down as a Stoic, or as one of the Old Academy — both he cannot be; for between them there is a contention not about boundaries but about the whole possession; for the whole reason of life is contained in the definition of the highest good, and those who disagree about it disagree about the whole reason of life; both, then, cannot be wise, since they so greatly dissent, but one — : if the Polemonian view is right, the Stoic errs, assenting to a false thing (and you yourselves say that nothing is so alien to the wise man); but if Zeno's things are true, the same must be said against the Old Academics and Peripatetics. Here, then, assenting to neither — if never — which is the more prudent?'

'What, when Antiochus himself dissents in certain matters from those Stoics whom he loves, does he not show that those things cannot be approved by the wise man? It pleases the Stoics that all sins are equal; but this displeases Antiochus most vehemently. Let it be allowed me at last to consider which opinion I shall follow. "Cut it short," he says, "determine at last upon something whatever it be." What, when the things that are said seem to me both acute on either side and equal, should I not beware lest I commit a crime? For you said, Lucullus, that it is a crime to betray a dogma; I restrain myself, then, lest I assent to the unknown, which is a dogma common to me with you.'

'Behold, a much greater dissension still. Zeno thinks the happy life is placed in virtue alone. What of Antiochus? "Happy too," he says, "but not the happiest." That god, who judged that nothing is wanting to virtue; this little man, who thinks that many things besides virtue are to a man partly dear, partly even necessary. But I fear both that the former assigns more to virtue than nature allows — especially as Theophrastus says many things eloquently and copiously — and I am afraid that the latter is scarcely consistent with himself, who, while he says that there are certain evils both of body and of fortune, yet judges that he who is in all these will be happy if he is wise: I am pulled apart; now this seems to me more probable, now that; and yet, unless one or the other be so, I plainly think that virtue lies prostrate. But in these things they disagree.'

'What of those things in which they agree — can we approve them as true: that the mind of the wise man is never moved by desire nor carried away by gladness? Come, let these be granted probable; what of those — never to fear, never to grieve: should the wise man not fear lest his country be destroyed, not grieve if it has been destroyed? Hard; but necessary for Zeno, to whom there is nothing among goods except the honourable; but for you, Antiochus, least of all, to whom, besides the honourable, many things seem goods, and besides baseness many things evils, which the wise man must necessarily both fear as they come and grieve at as having come. But I ask when these things were doctrines of the Old Academy — that they should deny that the mind of the wise man is moved and disturbed: they approved means, and wished there to be a certain natural measure in every emotion. We have all read the book of Crantor, the Old Academic, on grief; for it is not great, but a little golden one, and, as Panaetius advises Tubero, to be learned by heart word for word. And those men indeed even said that those emotions were given to our minds usefully by nature — fear for the sake of caution, pity and grief for the sake of mercy; anger itself they said was as it were the whetstone of courage — whether rightly or not we shall see another time; but how that severity of yours has broken into the Old Academy I do not know. But those things indeed I cannot bear — not that they displease me, for most of the marvels of the Stoics which are called paradoxa are Socratic; but where did Xenocrates, where did Aristotle touch those things (for you wish these to be as it were the same)? — would they ever say that the wise alone are kings, alone rich, alone fair; that all things everywhere are the wise man's; that no one is consul, praetor, general — I know not whether even one of the board of five — unless he be wise; finally, that he alone is a citizen, alone free, and that the unwise are all foreigners, exiles, slaves, in fine madmen; that the writings of Lycurgus, of Solon, our Twelve Tables are not laws, nor even is it a city or a state unless it be of the wise?'

'These things, Lucullus, if you have assented to your friend Antiochus, are to be defended by you as much as the walls; but by me only in moderation, only so far as shall seem good. I read in Clitomachus that, when Carneades and the Stoic Diogenes were standing before the senate on the Capitol, Aulus Albinus — who was then praetor, in the consulship of Publius Scipio and Marcus Marcellus, the man who was consul with your grandfather, Lucullus, a learned man indeed, as his own history written in Greek shows — said jestingly to Carneades: "I, Carneades, do not seem to you to be praetor, because I am not wise, nor this a city, nor in it a state?" Then he: "To this Stoic you do not seem so." Aristotle or Xenocrates, whom Antiochus wished to follow, would not have doubted that both that man was praetor and that Rome was a city and that a state dwelt in it; but that man of ours is plainly, as I said above, a Stoic stammering a very few things.'

'But you — to me, fearing lest I slip into opinion and adopt and approve something unknown, which you least of all wish — what counsel do you give? Chrysippus testifies often that there are only three opinions which can be defended about the ends of goods; he cuts down and lops off the multitude. For either the honourable is the end, or pleasure, or both. For those who say that the highest good is this, if we be free from all distress, flee the invidious name of pleasure but dwell in its neighbourhood; which those also do who joined that same thing with the honourable, and not much otherwise those who added to the honourable the first advantages of nature. So he leaves three opinions which he thinks can be defended with probability.'

'Let it be so indeed — although from the ends of Polemo and the Peripatetics and Antiochus I am not easily torn away, nor have I anything as yet more probable. Yet I see how sweetly pleasure flatters our senses; I am slipping to the point of assenting to Epicurus or Aristippus: virtue calls me back, or rather rebukes me with the hand, says those are the movements of cattle, and joins man to god. I can be in the middle, so that, since Aristippus, as though we had no soul, guards the body alone, while Zeno, as though we were devoid of body, embraces the soul alone, I should follow Callipho — whose opinion indeed Carneades so zealously kept defending that he even seemed to approve it; although Clitomachus affirmed that he could never understand what Carneades approved — but if I should wish to follow that very end, would not severity itself and gravity and right reason confront me: "Will you, when honour consists in the despising of pleasure, couple honour with pleasure as one couples a man with a beast?"'

'There remains, then, one pair to fight it out — pleasure with honour; about which, as far as I perceive, there is no great contention for Chrysippus. If you follow the one, many things fall, and most of all fellowship with the human race, affection, friendship, justice, and the rest of the virtues, of which there can be none unless it be gratuitous; for that which is impelled to duty by pleasure as by a kind of wage is not virtue but a deceitful imitation and pretence of virtue. Hear, on the other side, those who say that the very name of honour is not even understood by them (unless perhaps we should wish to call honourable that which is glorious in the eyes of the crowd), that the fountain of all goods is in the body, that this is the norm, this the rule, this the prescription of nature, from which whoever has strayed will never have anything to follow in life.'

'Do you think, then, that I am moved by nothing, when I hear these things and innumerable others? I am moved as much as you, Lucullus, and you should not think me less a man than yourself; only this is the difference, that you, when you are moved, adopt, assent, approve, and wish that to have been true, certain, comprehended, perceived, ratified, firm, fixed, and can by no reasoning be either driven or moved from it; whereas I think there is nothing of such a kind that, if I should assent to it, I should not often assent to a falsehood, since true things are separated from false by no distinction of impression — especially since those criteria of dialectic are nothing.'

'For I come now to the third part of philosophy. Different is the criterion of Protagoras, who thinks that to each that is true which seems so to each; different that of the Cyrenaics, who think there is no criterion except inner emotions; different that of Epicurus, who places all criterion in the senses and in the notions of things and in pleasure; but Plato wished that all judgement of truth, and truth itself, drawn away from opinions and from the senses, should belong to thought itself and to the mind.'

'Does our friend Antiochus approve any of these? Not even, indeed, that of his own elders. For where does he follow Xenocrates, whose books on the method of speaking are many and much approved, or Aristotle himself, than whom certainly nothing is more acute, nothing more polished? From Chrysippus he nowhere stirs a foot. We, then, who are called Academics (or do we abuse the glory of the name?) — or why are we compelled to follow those who disagree among themselves? In this very thing which the dialecticians teach in their elements — in what way one ought to judge whether it be true or false, if anything is so connected as this, "if it is day, it is light" — how great is the contention: it pleases Diodorus one way, Philo another, Chrysippus another. What of Chrysippus — in how many matters does he disagree with his own teacher Cleanthes? What of the two leaders, as it were, of the dialecticians, Antipater and Archidemus, most thorny men — do they not dissent in many matters?'

'Why, then, Lucullus, do you call me into ill-will and as it were into an assembly, and, as seditious tribunes are wont, order the shops to be closed? For to what does that tend, when you complain that the arts are taken away by us, except that the craftsmen may be stirred up — who, if from all sides they all come together, will easily be incited against you? I will first set forth those invidious things — that you say all those who stand in the assembly are exiles, slaves, madmen. Then I will come to those things which now pertain not to the multitude but to your own selves who are present. For Zeno denies, Antiochus denies, that you know anything. "How so?" you will say; "for we defend that even the unwise man comprehends many things."'

'But you deny that anyone knows any thing except the wise man. And this indeed Zeno used to set forth by a gesture. For when he had held out his hand with the fingers extended, "an impression," he would say, "is of this kind"; then when he had drawn the fingers in a little, "assent of this kind"; then when he had wholly closed it and made a fist, he said that was comprehension — from which likeness he even imposed on that thing the name, which it had not had before, katalepsis; but when he had brought his left hand to it and pressed that fist tightly and forcibly, he said that knowledge was of such a kind, of which no one was possessed except the wise man. But who is or has been wise not even they themselves are wont to say. So you now, Catulus, do not know that it is light, nor you, Hortensius, that we are in your villa.'

'Are these things said any less invidiously? Yet not too elegantly; those other things more subtly. But, just as you, if nothing could be comprehended, said that the arts collapse, nor granted me that the probable has force great enough for the arts, so I now bring back to you that there cannot be art without knowledge. Or would Zeuxis, or Phidias, or Polyclitus have endured this — that they knew nothing, when in them there was such great skill? But if someone had taught them how great a force knowledge was said to have, they would cease to be angry; nor would they be wroth even with us, when they had learned that we take away that which exists nowhere, but leave to them that which is enough. This method the diligence of our ancestors also approves, who first wished each man to swear according to the conviction of his own mind, then that he be held bound if he should knowingly deceive — because much ignorance is involved in life; then, that he who gave testimony should say that he thought so, even of what he himself had seen, and that the things which sworn judges had ascertained should be pronounced not as having been done or not done, but as seeming so.'

'But since not only the sailor signals but the west wind itself whispers to us, Lucullus, that it is time for us to sail, and since I have said enough, let me make an end. Hereafter, however, when we inquire into these matters, let us rather discourse about the so great dissensions of the highest men, about the obscurity of nature, and about the error of so many philosophers, who disagree so greatly about good and contrary things that — since more than one cannot be true — it is necessary that so many and so noble schools lie prostrate, rather than about the falsehoods of the eyes and of the rest of the senses, and about the sorites or the liar — those nets which the Stoics have woven against themselves.'

Then Lucullus said: 'I do not take it ill that we have compared these views. For meeting more often, and especially at our places near Tusculum, we shall inquire into whatever shall seem good.' 'Excellent,' said I; 'but what does Catulus think, what Hortensius?' Then Catulus said: 'I? I return to my father's opinion, which indeed he used to say was that of Carneades — that I think nothing can be perceived, yet judge that the wise man will assent to the unperceived, that is, will hold an opinion, but so that he understands that he is holding an opinion, and knows that there is nothing which can be comprehended and perceived. And so, while approving that withholding of assent in all things, I vehemently assent to that other opinion, that there is nothing which can be perceived.' 'I have your opinion,' said I, 'and I do not greatly spurn it. But what, pray, seems good to you, Hortensius?' Then he, laughing, said: 'It must be done away with.' 'I have you,' said I; 'for that is the Academy's own opinion.' The discourse thus finished, Catulus stayed behind, and we went down to our little boats.
